canonicalExplanation.summary: Data is split by job. The **training set** fits the model's parameters. The **validation set** (or **cross-validation**) guides your choices: which model, which settings. The **test set** is locked away and used **once**, at the end, to estimate how the finished procedure will do on new data. **Leakage** is any way information from the evaluation data sneaks into training, making scores look better than reality. Common kinds: **target leakage** (a feature only known after the outcome), **group leakage** (the same patient in train and test), **temporal leakage** (training on the future to predict the past) and **preprocessing leakage** (fitting scalers on all data). The split must **mimic deployment**: if you'll predict next month for new patients, test on later months and unseen patients.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner randomly splits hospital visits 80/20 and gets 97% accuracy. In deployment it drops to 71%. The same patients had visits in both train and test, so the model recognised people instead of learning patterns, and some test visits were earlier than training ones. All records for one patient stay in one split and the newest time period is held out when deployment predicts future visits. In this lesson you'll choose a split strategy and detect target, temporal, group or preprocessing leakage.

```predict
{"question": "The same patient's visits appear in both train and test. What happens to the test score?", "options": ["Nothing, rows are different", "It's inflated: the model can recognise the patient rather than generalise"], "answer": 1, "why": "Split by patient, not by row."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin

sections.heading: The rule: split the way you'll deploy
sections.body:
```python
visits = [  # (patient, month, outcome)
    ("p1", 1, 0), ("p1", 2, 1), ("p2", 1, 0), ("p3", 2, 1),
    ("p3", 3, 1), ("p4", 3, 0), ("p5", 4, 1), ("p5", 4, 0),
]

cutoff = 3                                        # predict the future: hold out newest months.
train = [v for v in visits if v[1] < cutoff]
test = [v for v in visits if v[1] >= cutoff]

train_patients = {p for p, *_ in train}
test = [v for v in test if v[0] not in train_patients]   # and unseen patients only.

print("train:", train)
print("test:", test)          # [('p4', 3, 0), ('p5', 4, 1), ('p5', 4, 0)]
print("overlap:", train_patients & {p for p, *_ in test})   # set()
```

| Leakage | Example | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| target. | discharge notes predicting admission. | only prediction-time features. |
| group. | same patient in both sets. | group split. |
| temporal. | future rows in training. | time-based split. |
| preprocessing. | scaler fit on all data. | fit inside training folds. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Why was p3's month-3 visit dropped from test?", "answer": "p3 appears in training (month 2). Keeping their later visit in test would let the model recognise them. Dropping it keeps the test about new patients."}
```

examples.title: The 97% that became 71%
examples.situation: A random row split gave 97% accuracy, but deployment on new patients scored 71%.
walkthrough: The same patients were in train and test, and some test rows were older than training ones.
Split by patient and by time instead.
Re-run: the test score drops to a realistic level before launch.
examples.result: The team sees the real score before deployment, not after.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Any random 80/20 split prevents leakage as long as the target column is removed from model inputs.
misconceptions.correction: Leakage also comes from repeated groups, time order, post-outcome features and preprocessing fitted on test data. The split must mirror deployment.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The 97% that became 71%", which two leaks inflated the score?

analogy.example: A test set is like **a final exam**. If students saw the **exact questions** in practice (group leakage), or the answer key was printed on the back of a practice sheet (target leakage), a high score means nothing. And if you rewrite your study plan every time you peek at the exam, it's **no longer a final exam**.
usefulFor: remembering don't see the exam questions early
limitations: A time split is testing on next year's exam, not last year's.

artifact: remove test patients seen in training
